artists.biography:
No-Man are an English art-pop duo formed in 1987 as No Man Is An Island (Except The Isle Of Man) by singer Tim Bowness and multi-instrumentalist Steven Wilson (the latter also of Porcupine Tree). The band has so far produced six studio albums and a number of singles/outtakes collections (most notably, 2006's career retrospective, All The Blue Changes). The band was once lauded as "conceivably the most important English group since The Smiths" by Melody Maker music newspaper.
Originally creating a sample-based proto-trip hop/ambient/electro-pop-styled music, No-Man has pursued a more organic, diverse and band-oriented sound in subsequent years. Drawing from a diverse mix of singer-songwriter, post rock, minimalist, progressive rock, jazz and contemporary ambient sources for inspiration, No-Man's musical style is distinctive yet difficult to categorise.

perplexity.description:
Flowermouth is the second studio album by British duo No-Man, released on 27 June 1994 on One Little Indian Records. Recorded between September and December 1993 at No Man's Land studio in Hemel Hempstead, the album blends trip hop, dream pop, and art rock into a sophisticated, experimental sound. Produced by Tim Bowness and Steven Wilson, the record showcases the duo's evolving approach to electronic and alternative music, incorporating ambient textures alongside more structured pop sensibilities.

The album marked a pivotal moment in No-Man's career trajectory. While the project was ambitious in scope and artistic vision, it presented significant commercial and critical challenges for the band. Despite these difficulties, the record demonstrated the duo's willingness to push beyond conventional boundaries, with melancholic and progressive arrangements that set it apart from mainstream electronic and rock releases of the era. The 57-minute album received mixed but generally favorable reviews, with publications like Melody Maker responding positively to its artistic ambitions.

Flowermouth has since been reissued multiple times, including a remastered edition in 1999 and a deluxe format release by Snapper Music in 2005, indicating sustained interest in the album's distinctive sonic palette. The record remains a notable entry in No-Man's discography, representing a period of creative experimentation that helped define the band's artistic identity during the 1990s.
